newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK CBANK SAYS ITS POLICY NOT RESTRICTIVE-PAPER.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK CBANK SAYS ITS POLICY NOT RESTRICTIVE-PAPER.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) rejects criticism that its monetary policy is too restrictive, the independent daily Narodna Obroda reported on Friday.

"One cannot talk about a restrictive policy as the central bank has been supporting economic growth by easing its monetary policy since the second half of 1994," NBS Governor Vladimir Masar told the paper.
The M2 aggregate, the key NBS yardstick for assesing the money supply, rose 15.5 percent year-on-year last year, down from a record level of 24.1 percent in March 1996.
The country's nominal gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 12.9 percent year-on-year in 1996.
NBS officials have often backed the bank's policy with the argument that over the past two years M2 growth has always exceeded nominal GDP growth.

The NBS has gradually adopted measures designed to rein in a rapidly growing money supply since last summer, eventually creating a liqidity shortage on the interbak market at the beginning of the year, pushing interbank money rates to record levels of above 26 percent several times.

High rates have sparked criticism from the industrial sector, banks and even the finance ministry, all of whom have called for policy loosening to ensure cheaper funds for further restructuring of the badly-undercapitalised Slovak economy.
The NBS, however, said it may not further ease monetary policy since this would make it difficult to keep inflation under control.

It also called for the government to reconsider some of its spending programmes scheduled for this year, saying they would drain funds that could be channelled into the economy and make it expensive to refinance the budget deficit forecast at 36.9 billion crowns.
